solutions.check: 30 entries; each light the paper's grid did not give solved here from its clue's wordplay (an anagram or hidden word, the one listed word fitting every crossing) and its definition (WordNet), agrees with the 29 answers the paper printed

clue.text: Is he entitled to be trodden underfoot?

definitions.text: Is he entitled to be trodden underfoot?

parts.words: Is he entitled to be trodden underfoot?
parts.note: reads as someone with a title who gets walked on, i.e. a knight whose name begins with a floor covering

explanation.surface: A question whether a titled man deserves to be walked all over.
explanation.walkthrough: A carpet knight is a knight dubbed at court, kneeling on a carpet, rather than on the battlefield: a stay-at-home soldier. 'Entitled' means holding a title, and carpets are trodden underfoot.
explanation.definitionFit: An old term of contempt for a courtier knighted for favour rather than valour in war.

clue.text: Fly-wheels are still here

parts.note: a fly was a light horse-drawn hire carriage; such wheels stand waiting at this place

explanation.surface: An engineering remark about machine flywheels standing motionless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly-wheels' looks like the machine part, but a fly was a hired horse carriage and wheels are vehicles: the place where hire vehicles stand still is a taxi stand.
explanation.definitionFit: A taxi stand where hire vehicles wait for passengers.

clue.text: Truly this is a test of sobriety

definitions.text: Truly this is a test of sobriety

parts.words: Truly this is a test of sobriety
parts.note: the tongue-twister 'truly ...' is a way to check whether someone has been drinking

explanation.surface: A claim that something is really a check on whether someone is drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Truly rural' is a classic tongue-twister that a drunk person cannot say clearly; 'Truly' looks like an adverb but is the first word of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means countryside-related, and with truly forms a tongue-twister drunks fail.

clue.text: But a middleman in business could be this in politics

definitions.text: But a middleman in business could be this in politics

parts.words: But a middleman in business could be this in politics
parts.note: a commercial go-between stands in the middle, whereas in politics the person meant stands at the far ends

explanation.surface: A remark contrasting the role of a trade intermediary with a political one.
explanation.walkthrough: In politics the middle ground belongs to moderates, so a middleman there would be a moderate; the clue plays on the opposite, someone at the far edge of opinion.
explanation.definitionFit: A person holding radical political views far from the centre ground.

clue.text: Taking without thanks, he cannot be taken

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letters for thanks are removed from the word before

parts.note: ta is informal British for thank you

explanation.surface: Someone who grabs things ungratefully yet is himself untouchable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes TA from TAKING. In chess the king is never captured: the game ends at checkmate first.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess the monarch piece is never actually captured; checkmate ends the game.

clue.text: Macbeth thought he was doomed to suffer from it

definitions.text: Macbeth thought he was doomed to suffer from it

parts.words: Macbeth thought he was doomed to suffer from it
parts.note: recalls the voice crying 'Macbeth shall sleep no more' after the murder of Duncan

explanation.surface: A remark about the affliction Shakespeare's Macbeth feared.
explanation.walkthrough: After killing Duncan, Macbeth hears a voice cry 'Macbeth does murder sleep... Macbeth shall sleep no more'.
explanation.definitionFit: Habitual sleeplessness, which Macbeth believed was his punishment.

clue.text: Outcome of shell-bursts

parts.note: reads as the effect of exploding artillery, but the shells are eggs breaking open as chicks emerge

explanation.surface: The aftermath of an artillery bombardment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shell-bursts' suggests artillery, but it is eggshells breaking as chicks come out.
explanation.definitionFit: A brood of young birds emerging from eggs at one time.

clue.text: Fish I catch for the little ones

parts.note: the bass is a sea fish
to net something is to catch it

explanation.surface: An angler saying the fish he catches are for his children.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: a bassinet is something for babies.
explanation.definitionFit: A hooded wicker cradle or basket used for newborn babies.

clue.text: The capital of Spain is the subject of an essay

indicators.note: capital means the first, capital letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Madrid as the topic for a school essay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The capital of Spain' wants to be Madrid; 'capital of' only takes the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A proposition put forward and argued in a dissertation or essay.

clue.text: Singers ain't sober when fuddled

indicators.note: fuddled means drunk and muddled, so the letters of the words before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: Vocalists who are only sober-looking once they have had a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when fuddled' rearranges AINTSOBER.
explanation.definitionFit: Baritones are male voices pitched between tenor and bass, so they are a kind of vocalist.

clue.text: Iago considered his purse to be

definitions.text: Iago considered his purse to be

parts.words: Iago considered his purse to be
parts.note: recalls Iago's line in Othello about a stolen purse being worthless stuff

explanation.surface: A question about what Shakespeare's villain thought of his money.
explanation.walkthrough: In Othello Iago says 'Who steals my purse steals trash'.
explanation.definitionFit: Iago calls his purse worthless rubbish in a famous speech about reputation.

clue.text: Cooperators, fifty-one of them, get drinks all round

indicators.note: the drinks are said to go all round the number, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: ales are drinks of beer
LI is fifty-one in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Fifty-one partners buying rounds of drinks for one another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all round' puts the ALES round LI. The page prints 'Co-operators'.
explanation.definitionFit: Allies are parties who work together towards a shared aim, as partners do.

clue.text: Stress can misshape letters

indicators.note: the clue says the letters of the word misshape can be rearranged to give the answer

explanation.surface: Putting too much stress on a thing can bend letters out of shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misshape' looks like the verb, but it is the fodder; 'letters' signals that its letters are reordered.
explanation.definitionFit: Emphasis is the stress laid on a word or point to mark its importance.

clue.text: Gee up from the loch — that's the spirit

definitions.meaning: a gee-gee is a horse, here one rising from a Scottish lake
a spirit in the sense of a ghostly or supernatural being

explanation.surface: Someone urging a horse on and cheering it, as if beside a Scottish lake.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scottish folklore the kelpie is a water spirit that takes the shape of a horse and haunts lochs (Scottish lakes). 'Gee up' looks like a command to a horse, but here a gee is the horse itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves describe the Scottish water demon in equine form, a horse-like ghost of lakes.

clue.text: Equality for all, his down-to-earth policy

definitions.text: Equality for all, his down-to-earth policy

parts.words: Equality for all, his down-to-earth policy
parts.note: describes a person who wants to make everyone equal, bringing the high down to earth

explanation.surface: A sensible, practical politician promising equal treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: The Levellers were radicals of the English Civil War who wanted equal rights; one who levels things brings them down to the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: One who seeks to abolish social distinctions and make all ranks equal.

clue.text: Conifers yield them, naturally

indicators.note: naturally suggests the word conifers rearranging itself, as by nature, into new order

explanation.surface: Coniferous trees produce their seed cases as a matter of course.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, and 'naturally' also signals the rearrangement of CONIFERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Pines and firs bear woody seed cones, the fruit of these evergreen trees.

clue.text: One thing I can never be, literally

definitions.text: One thing I can never be, literally

parts.words: One thing I can never be, literally
parts.note: taken literally, the letter I is a vowel, so it can never be the other type of letter

explanation.surface: A confession of something a person could never become.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' looks like the speaker, but it is the letter I, a vowel; 'literally' points to letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The letter I is a vowel, so it can never be a non-vowel speech sound or letter.

clue.text: He avoided growing pains

parts.note: growing pains are aches of adolescence; the boy meant never grew up at all

explanation.surface: A man who escaped the aches of adolescence.
explanation.walkthrough: J. M. Barrie's boy who never grew up never had growing pains.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrie's hero refuses to grow up, so he never suffers the aches of growing.

clue.text: Tots gave a variety of dances

indicators.note: a variety of means a mixed arrangement, so the letters of the words before it are reordered

explanation.surface: Small children performing an assortment of dances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a variety of' rearranges TOTSGAVE.
explanation.definitionFit: The gavotte is an old French court dance in moderate four-time.

clue.text: Fishes look astonished

parts.note: a fish or shellfish named for its open-mouthed look, as people stare with mouths open

explanation.surface: Fish with their mouths open look surprised.
explanation.walkthrough: Gapers are fishes and clams named for gaping; a gaper is also a person staring open-mouthed.
explanation.definitionFit: Gapers are fish and clams named for their open mouths, as gawpers stare.

clue.text: How to march correctly on foot

definitions.meaning: soldiers should march keeping pace together, the phrase read as two words
the arched top part of the human foot

explanation.surface: Instructions for marching properly, on foot.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words it is how to march; as one, it is part of the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Marching in step means keeping pace with the others; the instep is the arched middle of the foot.

clue.text: Quiet man in front is an advocate

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet
the one in front is the leader

explanation.surface: A soft-spoken man at the head of things is a lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: P for quiet comes from piano in music.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleader argues a case in court on someone's behalf, as an advocate does.

clue.text: Growth in desert? Can magician do it, given a big hand?

definitions.meaning: a plant that grows at an oasis

definitions.text: Can magician do it, given a big hand?
definitions.meaning: a conjuror hides small objects in the hand, so a huge hand might hide a whole tree

explanation.surface: Musing about desert plants and whether a conjuror with a huge hand could make one vanish.
explanation.walkthrough: To palm something is to hide it in the hand, a conjuror's trick; with a big enough hand he could palm a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The date palm is the classic oasis plant; to palm a tree is a conjuring sleight on a large scale.

clue.text: Thessaly's beauty spot starts a dramatic storm

indicators.note: the answer is only how the word starts, so its last letters are cut

parts.note: The Tempest is Shakespeare's play opening with a storm

explanation.surface: A Greek scenic place where a theatrical storm begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts' takes the start of TEMPEST, removing ST. The Vale of Tempe in Thessaly, Greece, was famed in classical times for its beauty.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vale of Tempe is a celebrated gorge in northern Greece, famous for its scenery.

clue.text: This crossing is treacherous

parts.note: not a dangerous road crossing but betrayal, a cross made twice over

explanation.surface: A warning about a perilous road or river crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: Double-crossing is betraying someone, so the 'crossing' that is treacherous is a double one.
explanation.definitionFit: A double-cross is a betrayal, deceiving someone one appears to be helping.

clue.text: Here Tom Bowling was faithful, and did his duty

definitions.text: Here Tom Bowling was faithful, and did his duty

parts.words: Here Tom Bowling was faithful, and did his duty
parts.note: quotes Dibdin's sea song, in which the sailor was faithful in this place before going aloft

explanation.surface: An epitaph for a loyal man called Tom Bowling.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Dibdin's song 'Tom Bowling' says 'Faithful, below, he did his duty, But now he's gone aloft': below is the sailor's word for under decks, and aloft means heaven.
explanation.definitionFit: On a ship, below means under the decks; in the song it also means here on earth.

clue.text: Surely singularly inappropriate for a feast ?

definitions.text: Surely singularly inappropriate for a feast ?

parts.words: Surely singularly inappropriate for a feast ?
parts.note: a ... is a jolly party, yet a single legume would make a meagre meal

explanation.surface: A doubt whether some food is fit for a banquet.
explanation.walkthrough: A beanfeast is a British word for a party or annual works outing; one single bean would hardly feed anyone.
explanation.definitionFit: A single seed of a legume, which joins with feast to name a celebration.

clue.text: He is in drink, hence the ill-humour

indicators.note: the clue says he is in the drink, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: rum is a spirit drink
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man who drinks too much, which explains his bad mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts HE inside RUM. 'Ill-humour' looks like bad temper, but in old medicine a humour was a bodily fluid: here a watery discharge.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheum is a watery discharge from eyes or nose, one of the unhealthy fluids of old medicine.

clue.text: What Victor did

parts.note: reads as the deeds of a man called Victor, but a victor is any winner

explanation.surface: A question about the actions of someone named Victor.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital V makes Victor look like a name; a victor is simply whoever wins.
explanation.definitionFit: A winner is one who has triumphed, overcoming the opposition.

clue.text: No winter gale can wreck this campanile

indicators.note: wreck means smash up, so the letters of the words before it are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A bell tower so sturdy no winter storm can bring it down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can wreck' rearranges NOWINTERGALE. The Pisa tower has leant for centuries without falling.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous tilted bell tower at Pisa is a campanile, an Italian free-standing belfry.
